description: Collecting data from sources and conducting stimulations
summary: Project Hypothesis is a free interactive story map of NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars, built for school age space fans. Students pick a site, such as Apollo 11's descent stage, the Apollo lunar rovers, Spirit, Opportunity, or Ingenuity, and make a "hypothesis" \\pun intended\\ about what happened to the hardware and what it left behind. They then reveal the real story of why it was left there, what science it made possible, and what condition it is in now, shown with NASA orbiter images. We also include ISRO's Chandrayaan-2 Vikram lander as a link to our What it does: A Moon/Mars map with a clickable card for each piece of hardware: Mission, Why it was left, What it discovered, and Its status today. It'll reveal details about it as you interact with the hardware pieces.
details:
What it does: "Project Hypothesis is a free interactive explorer for the challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten". It covers nine pieces of hardware left on, or lost at, the Moon and Mars: the Apollo 15, 16 and 17 Lunar Roving Vehicles, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity and ISRO's Chandrayaan-2 Vikram lander. Each mission has a brief with launch date, objectives and status. Students tap glowing parts of a code-drawn vehicle, such as wheels, antennas, arms and engines, to learn what each does and why it mattered. It tells the story of equipment left behind, including failures like Vikram's lost landing. It runs offline on phones and school computers with no login. Code, illustrations and text were generated with an AI chatbot (Claude) and reviewed by our team


How it works: Each vehicle is a clickable diagram built from inline SVG, split into hotspots such as wheels, antennas, solar panels, robotic arms and engines. Mission data is stored in one structured set of records, so every mission shares the same layout and adding a new one is easy.

Benefits and impact: It turns "abandoned" hardware into stories about why a machine was left behind, what it discovered, and what engineers learned, from sand traps and dust storms to a landing that failed. It works on phones and school computers with almost no internet connection. so classrooms with weak connectivity can use it if they logged into SI used. so it links past missions to today's mars efforts and makes it accessible to people.

Creative approach: It covers both the Moon and Mars, and includes Chandrayaan-2 Vikram so the story isn't only about NASA. Failures are treated as part of the story. The drawings are code-made, so nothing depends on copyrighted or branded imagery.

Tools: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or external files. It runs as one file, hosted on GitHub Pages or opened directly from a device. Facts were checked against NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, the NASA Mars Exploration Program and Other Space Agency Datas.

Factors considered: Accessibility (keyboard-navigable hotspots, reduced-motion support), mobile-first layout, offline use, and accuracy over detail, with simplified schematics clearly labelled for deeper understanding.

SI Awareness: We used an AI chatbot (Claude) to help generate the code and draft the component descriptions, and we reviewed the content against NASA and Other sources
